 A Product Recall Playbook for Food and Supplement Brands
 Author(s) Brad Staubus , Niyati Patel Listen 0:00 / 0:00 Key Takeaways
 Recall outcomes are often determined by misaligned contracts, documentation, and insurance rather than the underlying quality event, creating avoidable disputes over authority, records, and cost recovery. 
 Rapid stabilization requires distribution freezes, SKU/lot identification, inventory segregation, and immediate clarification of contract manufacturer control over traceability, quarantine authority, and external communications. 
 Early, centralized FDA communications reduce escalation risk and recall scope, while brand–manufacturer misalignment on terminology, timing, and messaging can trigger prolonged oversight and insurer concern. 
 Insurance recovery depends on Day 0 notice, written consent practices before destruction or major spend, and rigorous contemporaneous documentation, including lot traceability, invoices, retailer deductions, and a recall-specific ledger. 
 Prevention hinges on supply/manufacturing agreements that specify recall initiation authority, cost allocation, recall insurance requirements, robust indemnities, audit/record access, and a tested recall SOP covering first-week actions.
 SHOW MORE Common pitfalls and important precautions that will make dealing with recalls more manageable. 
 Advertisement Product recalls are some of the most disruptive and financially significant events a food or supplement brand can experience. They are the ultimate "stress test." In a matter of days, a single quality deviation can spark a chain reaction of retailer disputes, regulatory scrutiny, supply-chain breakdowns, and financial exposure. Many brands overlook the fact that recalls are more than just operational issues. The brands that suffer the most are rarely those with the most serious underlying problem; rather, those whose contracts, documentation, and insurance programs were never designed to work together under pressure.
Common pitfalls include:
 No recall insurance, or insufficient recall coverage
 Inconsistent understanding between the brand and the contract manufacturer regarding recall initiation, roles, and responsibilities
 Delayed notice to insurers while “facts are still developing”
 Product destruction before insurer or third-party or contract manufacturer approval
 Incomplete or reconstructed lot-level records
 Contract manufacturer insurance that exists on paper but fails in practice
 These gaps don’t always stop a recall, but they often determine whether costs are recoverable.
 This article outlines:
 The first 24 hours— establishing control and preserving options
 Insurance preservation and recovery— protecting coverage while costs escalate
 Prevention— why strong supply and contract manufacturing agreements determine recall economics long before a crisis begins
 The First 24 Hours 
 The first day of a recall sets the tone for insurer cooperation and internal confidence and alignment. At this stage, the goal is not to have all the answers. It’s to establish control, document decisions, and preserve options.
 Immediate Stabilization 
 Freeze distribution of potentially affected product
 Identify impacted: SKUs
 Lot or batch codes
 Production dates
 Distribution channels
 Physically and digitally segregate inventory
 The Contract Manufacturer Check 
 For contract manufactured products, brands must immediately confirm:
 Who controls lot-level and batch records
 Who has authority to quarantine inventory
 Who communicates with retailers and regulators
 If the contract manufacturer agreement is unclear, brands often lose valuable time negotiating authority mid-crisis—exactly when insurers and regulators expect decisive action.
 Regulatory Engagement: Dealing with FDA Early and Deliberately 
 For food and dietary supplement brands, recall execution does not occur in a vacuum. FDA engagement is often unavoidable, even in recalls initiated voluntarily. How and when the FDA is notified—and who controls that interaction—can materially affect recall scope, timing, and downstream insurance and liability exposure.
 Key principles:
 Voluntary recalls are still FDA-facing events. Even when a recall is not mandated, FDA expects timely notification once a firm determines that a product presents a risk or may violate the law.
 FDA communications should be centralized and controlled. Brands should designate a single regulatory lead—typically legal or quality—to manage all FDA interactions. Fragmented or inconsistent communications (especially between the brand and the contract manufacturer) create credibility issues and expand regulatory scrutiny.
 Early engagement preserves optionality. Proactive, well-documented communication with FDA can help: Avoid escalation
 Narrow recall scope
 Reduce the risk of FDA-imposed timelines or public enforcement actions
 Practical considerations in the first 24 hours:
 Identify which entity will communicate with FDA (brand vs. contract manufacturer)
 Align brand and contract manufacturer on facts, terminology, and timing before any FDA contact
 Preserve written records of all FDA communications
 Ensure recall actions are consistent with FDA guidance and recall classifications
 Misalignment between brand and contract manufacturer communications with FDA is a common and avoidable cause of expanded recalls, prolonged oversight, and insurer concern.
 Centralize Recall Leadership 
 Recalls fail when decisions are fragmented. Successful brands move quickly to a centralized command structure that treats the recall as a single, coordinated event—not a series of disconnected problems.
 Create a core recall command team that includes:
 Operations & supply chain
 Quality & food safety
 Legal & regulatory
 Finance & accounting
 Customer & retailer management
 Public Relations / Crisis Communications
 (internal or external; messaging coordinated with legal, regulatory, and insurer requirements) 
 Risk management / insurance broker
 Contract manufacturer representatives (as appropriate)
 This group is responsible not only for logistics, but also for:
 Approving recall-related spending
 Preserving claim documentation
 Ensuring actions align with insurance conditions
 Unilateral decisions, especially around destruction or vendor engagement, are one of the fastest ways to create coverage disputes.
 Recall Insurance Preservation Checklist 
 Insurance recovery is not automatic. It is earned through fast and diligent notice, documentation, and decision-making. Since insurance coverage can vary significantly by policy, a careful review of policy terms is critical. Consult with legal counsel if needed.
 Immediate Insurance Notice (Day 0) 
 One of the most common recall mistakes is treating insurance notice as a formality. In reality, notice timing is often a condition of coverage. Insurers expect notice even when facts are evolving. Late notice is routinely raised as a coverage defense, especially where early recall costs are significant. Do not wait for cost clarity, root-cause confirmation, or fault allocation.
 astro-island:empty]:hidden [&:has(>astro-island:empty)+*]:-mt-8"> Notify insurance broker and all potentially implicated insurers immediately, including: Recall / contamination
 General liability
 Property
 Business interruption
 Provide written notice of: A recall event or
 Circumstances reasonably likely to give rise to a claim
 Confirm applicable policy numbers, sub-limits, and assigned adjuster(s)
 Insurer Consent & Control 
 Many recall policies condition reimbursement on insurer consent, even where consent requirements are not explicit. Destruction of product without approval frequently shifts the evidentiary burden to the insured and invites disputes over quantity, valuation, and necessity.
 Confirm whether insurer approval is required before: Product destruction or disposal. Best practice would also be to notify the contract manufacturers and other potentially responsible parties.
 Remediation or rework
 Crisis-management or PR engagement. Some policies require the brand to contact the insurer’s crisis management hotline first. If not, they may lose coverage for outside PR engagement.
 Significant storage, transportation, or logistics costs
 Hiring a forensic accountant
 Submit approval requests in writing, with scope, rationale, and cost estimates Preserve written responses (or lack thereof)
 If immediate action is required: Memorialize urgency and operational necessity
 Document attempts to reach insurer
 Preserve product, samples, and records wherever feasible
 Centralized Documentation (Real-Time) 
 Insurers cross-check lot traceability against claimed quantities across returns, inventory on hand, and destroyed product.
 Establish a secure recall documentation repository
 Preserve contemporaneous records for: Lot-level traceability and production
 Inventory counts and segregation
 Retailer and customer communications
 Returns, deductions, and chargebacks
 Storage, transport, and destruction
 Regulatory correspondence
 Crisis management and PR costs
 Business interruption support
 Preserve detailed production and distribution records for all impacted lot codes. For contract manufactured products, obtain real-time lot and production data, not post-hoc summaries.
 Financial Tracking Discipline 
 Meticulous financial tracking allows insurers to distinguish recall-specific loss from normal operating cost and to evaluate allocation between brand and contract manufacturer.
 Create a recall-specific general ledger account
 Route all recall-related costs through this account.
 Create sub-accounts aligned with insurance categories, such as Customer deductions
 Fines, fees, and penalties
 Damaged or destroyed inventory
 Notification and PR
 Storage, transportation, and destruction
 Incremental payroll
 Track costs by SKU, lot code, and time period
 Business Interruption & Lost Sales 
 Business interruption claims fail most often due to weak causation, not lack of loss.
 Maintain a detailed recall chronology, including recall notice date, shelf-pull timing, duration until replacement product availability, and retailer decisions not to relist SKUs
 Preserve pre-recall forecasts, sales trends, backlog, and market data
 Track: Order cancellations
 De-listings or pauses
 Production disruptions
 Outsourced or alternate production
 Cost Substantiation: Returns, Inventory, & Recall Execution Expenses 
 Insurers scrutinize recall claims most heavily at the cost level. Over-inclusive customer deductions, unsupported inventory valuations, and poorly documented logistics or PR expenses are the most common sources of disputes.
 Segregate recall-related costs from routine business activity, including: Customer returns and deductions
 Impacted inventory
 Crisis management, PR, and incremental payroll
 Storage, transportation, and destruction
 Validate customer deductions and returns by confirming: Product description, SKU, and lot code
 Units returned or destroyed
 Deduction amounts align with purchase history and reasonable inventory levels
 Deductions fall within the actual recall scope
 Confirm contractual entitlement for fines, fees, lost profits, or chargebacks by reviewing applicable customer agreements and obtaining backup calculations where possible.
 Preserve and document impacted inventory, including: Perpetual inventory as of the date of loss
 Post-loss physical counts
 Insurer-approved disposal only
 Clear identification of non-impacted product returned by customers
 Apply the correct inventory valuation methodology under the policy (sales value vs. cost) and maintain supporting write-off documentation.
 Document recall-specific execution costs, including: PR or crisis-management engagements (Statements of work and detailed invoices)
 Incremental payroll tied exclusively to recall activity (time records required)
 Incremental storage, transportation, and destruction costs with detailed invoices and, where applicable, certificates of destruction
 Insurers reimburse incremental, recall-specific loss—not normal operating expense. Where brands accept borderline customer deductions to preserve retailer relationships, that judgment call should be explicitly documented.
 Insurance recovery is not about perfect outcomes. It is about defensible decisions.
 Recall Prevention Checklist: Strong Supply and Contract Manufacturing Agreements 
 Many recall disputes are not resolved during the recall itself. They are resolved by what the supply and contract manufacturing agreement already says. Strong contract manufacturing agreements function as an extension of the brand’s insurance policy. Review your supply and contract manufacturing agreements to ensure:
 Recall Authority, Coordination & Control 
 Agreement clearly defines the process for recall initiation, escalation, and coordination between the brand and the contract manufacturer.
 Agreement specifies who controls communications with: Insurers
 Regulators
 Retailers
 Consumers
 Product destruction, disposal, and remediation require: Brand approval
 Insurer approval where required
 Allocation of Recall Costs 
 Agreement expressly allocates responsibility for: Product retrieval and logistics
 Storage and disposal
 Testing and investigation
 Retailer chargebacks
 Customer deduction
 Penalties and fines
 Allocation framework is agreed upon, such as Fault-based
 Strict liability
 Shared responsibility
 Ensure agreement upon all material recall cost categories. Silence here often forces brands to absorb recall costs upfront with limited recovery leverage.
 Insurance Alignment 
 Contract Manufacturer is required to maintain product recall insurance
 General liability alone is not treated as sufficient
 Agreement specifies: Minimum coverage limits
 Acceptable carriers
 Coverage scope aligned with brand policy
 Brand is named as an additional insured where appropriate
 Waivers of subrogation included where commercially reasonable
 Ongoing proof of insurance required (certificates + renewals)
 Indemnification 
 Indemnity language must go beyond generic defect or negligence provisions
 Indemnity provisions explicitly reference: Recalls
 Market withdrawals
 Regulatory actions
 Indemnity covers: Retailer deductions and chargebacks
 Government-mandated recalls
 Third-party claims tied to recall events
 Recall indemnities survive termination of the agreement
 Indemnity language goes beyond generic defect or negligence provisions
 Operational Cooperation & Records 
 Contract Manufacturer is required to provide: Real-time lot and batch records
 Traceability documentation upon request
 Brand has audit and access rights during recall events
 No unilateral product destruction without brand approval
 One Action Item Brands Can Take Now 
 Adopt a written Recall Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) 
 A recall SOP is the single most effective way to align operations, regulatory response, contracts, and insurance before a crisis. It should be short, practical, and executable—not aspirational.
 At minimum, a recall SOP should include:
 Trigger criteria for recall vs. market withdrawal
 Step-by-step actions for the first 24, 72, and 7 days
 Defined authority and escalation paths between the brand and the contract manufacturer
 FDA engagement process, including who communicates and when
 Insurance notification and consent requirements
 Rules around product holds, destruction, and documentation
 Centralized decision-making and approval controls
 Required records and lot-level documentation
 Brands that wait to define recall procedures during a crisis are forced to improvise under regulatory and insurer scrutiny. Brands with a tested SOP act decisively, preserve coverage, and control outcomes.
 Key Takeaway 
 Recalls are inevitable. Financial chaos is not. Brands that recover most effectively treat recall preparedness as structural, not reactive. When operations, insurance, and contract manufacturer agreements are aligned before a crisis, recalls become manageable events. The real work of recall recovery happens long before the first product is pulled from shelves.
